stem:
A 58-year-old woman on lithium carbonate 750 mg nocte for bipolar I disorder presents to ED after 48 hours of gastroenteritis. She reports coarse tremor, unsteady gait and confusion. Her GP started ramipril 5 mg daily three weeks ago for hypertension. She has taken her usual lithium dose each morning. The intern has already given 1 L normal saline over one hour. A 12-hour post-dose lithium level returns while you are reviewing her.

She is drowsy but rousable, coarse tremor in both hands, brisk reflexes and bilateral horizontal nystagmus. Speech is dysarthric.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% on air, temp 36.8.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), coarse tremor, hyperreflexia, nystagmus, dysarthria.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 3.1 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8), creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 78), eGFR 32, sodium 142, potassium 4.4, urea 12.6.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Withhold lithium, continue IV normal saline at 200 mL/h, and repeat a level in six hours before deciding on further escalation
options.rationale: Saline is core supportive care but is inadequate as sole management given level >2.5 mmol/L with neurological features and acute kidney injury; delaying dialysis risks progression to seizures, coma and permanent cerebellar injury (SILENT). (Source: TG Psychotropic: Lithium toxicity)

options.text: Give a single dose of activated charcoal 50 g via nasogastric tube and admit to a ward bed for six-hourly level and neurological observations
options.rationale: Charcoal does not bind lithium (a monovalent cation) and there is no role for gut decontamination in chronic toxicity; a ward bed underestimates the required level of care for a patient with GCS 13 and progressive neurotoxicity. (Source: AMH: Lithium)

options.text: Urgent referral for extracorporeal treatment with haemodialysis, alongside IV fluids and cessation of lithium and ramipril, with HDU monitoring
options.rationale: EXTRIP consensus and Australian toxicology practice recommend extracorporeal treatment when lithium is >4.0 mmol/L in any patient, or >2.5 mmol/L with impaired kidney function or significant neurological features (reduced consciousness, seizures, life-threatening dysrhythmia). This patient meets both the level and the AKI-plus-neurology criteria. (Source: EXTRIP lithium recommendations; PIC 13 11 26)

options.text: Commence a forced alkaline diuresis with sodium bicarbonate infusion targeting a urinary pH above 7.5 to accelerate lithium clearance safely
options.rationale: Urinary alkalinisation is used in salicylate toxicity, not lithium; it does not accelerate lithium excretion and adds a sodium and volume burden that is not indicated here. (Source: TG Toxicology; PIC 13 11 26)

options.text: Start intravenous diazepam infusion for the neurological features and admit for observation while awaiting spontaneous renal clearance of lithium
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are only indicated if seizures occur; they do not address the underlying lithium burden and mask deteriorating consciousness. Spontaneous renal clearance is too slow in AKI. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)

explanation.summary: This is chronic lithium toxicity precipitated by ACE inhibitor commencement plus volume depletion from gastroenteritis. The level (3.1) is between 2.5 and 4.0, but AKI and neurotoxicity together are stand-alone dialysis triggers under EXTRIP guidance. Delaying dialysis to give more saline risks Syndrome of Irreversible Lithium-Effectuated Neurotoxicity (SILENT).
key_points: EXTRIP: dialyse if lithium >4.0, or >2.5 with reduced consciousness, seizures, life-threatening arrhythmia, or impaired renal function
ACEi/ARB, NSAIDs, thiazides and dehydration all reduce lithium clearance
Charcoal does not bind lithium; alkaline diuresis is not indicated
Continuous venovenous haemodiafiltration is acceptable when intermittent HD is unavailable
explanation.pearls: In context: any lithium level above 2.5 mmol/L with neurology or AKI is a dialysis conversation; do not wait for the level to climb past 4.

subtopic_detail: NSAID, ACEi and thiazide interactions in general practice
stem:
A 44-year-old man with bipolar I disorder stable on lithium 500 mg bd (last level 0.7 mmol/L four weeks ago) attends his GP with a two-week history of low back pain after moving house. He asks what over-the-counter or short-course prescription options are safe, given previous good response to ibuprofen. His BP today is 138/86 with normal renal function.

He drinks 1.5 L of water daily, takes no other medications, and has no history of peptic ulcer disease.

data_table.Examination: Paraspinal muscle spasm L4-L5, no red flags, neurologically intact.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 76 micromol/L, eGFR >90, sodium 140, potassium 4.2, lithium 0.7 mmol/L (four weeks ago).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate analgesic plan?

options.text: Recommend regular ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for two weeks with a check lithium level in one week and adjustment of dose thereafter as clinically indicated
options.rationale: NSAIDs reduce renal lithium clearance by up to 40% via reduced prostaglandin-mediated GFR; even short courses can push levels into the toxic range. Not appropriate to initiate ibuprofen. (Source: AMH: Lithium interactions)

options.text: Prescribe celecoxib 200 mg daily as a COX-2 selective agent that avoids the lithium interaction seen with non-selective NSAIDs in maintenance therapy
options.rationale: COX-2 selective agents interact with lithium via the same mechanism as non-selective NSAIDs and are not a workaround; AMH lists the interaction for the whole class. (Source: AMH: Lithium interactions)

options.text: Recommend regular paracetamol with heat, gentle mobilisation and physiotherapy referral; avoid all NSAIDs while on lithium therapy, and review at one week
options.rationale: Paracetamol has no lithium interaction and is first line for mechanical back pain; NSAIDs (including COX-2 selective) are relatively contraindicated as they raise lithium levels unpredictably. (Source: AMH: Lithium; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Add a low-dose thiazide diuretic to reduce lithium excretion and allow a lower lithium dose while treating incidental hypertension at the same visit
options.rationale: Thiazides reduce lithium clearance and are a well-documented cause of toxicity; deliberately combining them to reduce dose is unsafe and not a recognised strategy. (Source: AMH: Lithium interactions)

options.text: Prescribe a short course of oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for five days for anti-inflammatory effect while continuing his usual lithium regimen at home
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are not first line for mechanical back pain and carry mood-destabilising risk in bipolar disorder; not an appropriate substitute for simple analgesia. (Source: TG Rheumatology; RANZCP Mood CPG)

explanation.summary: NSAIDs (including COX-2 selective), ACE inhibitors, ARBs, thiazides and dehydration all reduce renal lithium clearance and are the commonest causes of chronic toxicity in stable outpatients. Paracetamol is the safe first line.
key_points: NSAIDs can raise lithium levels 20-40%
COX-2 selective agents interact the same way
Thiazides reduce clearance; loop diuretics have less effect but still monitor
If NSAID unavoidable, monitor level within 5-7 days and adjust dose
explanation.pearls: In context: any new NSAID, ACEi/ARB, thiazide or GI illness in a lithium patient is a level-check trigger.

subtopic_detail: Dose adjustment and monitoring frequency with declining eGFR
stem:
A 66-year-old man with bipolar I disorder has been on lithium 750 mg nocte for 22 years, with excellent mood stability and no admissions in the past decade. Routine annual bloods show eGFR has fallen from 68 to 42 mL/min/1.73m^2 over 18 months. His last lithium level (four weeks ago) was 0.85 mmol/L. Urinalysis is bland, ACR normal, ultrasound shows no obstruction.

He has type 2 diabetes on metformin and takes perindopril 5 mg for hypertension.

data_table.Examination: No signs of lithium toxicity, no volume overload.
data_table.Investigations: Lithium 0.85 mmol/L (target 0.6-0.8 for maintenance), creatinine 148 (baseline 96), eGFR 42, HbA1c 51 mmol/mol, ACR 1.2 mg/mmol.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue current dose; recheck lithium level and renal function in 12 months in line with routine outpatient monitoring schedule for this patient
options.rationale: Falling eGFR with a level at the upper end of target requires action, not routine annual review; RANZCP recommends 3-monthly levels once monitoring becomes more intensive. (Source: RANZCP Mood CPG)

options.text: Reduce lithium dose targeting 0.4-0.6 mmol/L, increase to 3-monthly levels and 6-monthly renal function, and involve psychiatry, monitor closely
options.rationale: In older adults and those with reduced eGFR, aim for a lower maintenance target (often 0.4-0.6) with more frequent monitoring; involve psychiatry regarding balance between mood stability and long-term nephrotoxicity, but abrupt cessation risks relapse. (Source: RANZCP Mood CPG; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease lithium immediately and commence sodium valproate 500 mg bd as a renally safer mood stabiliser starting this evening as a same-day switch
options.rationale: Abrupt lithium cessation carries a high relapse risk (up to 50% within 6 months) and rebound mania; any switch requires slow cross-titration and shared decision-making, not a same-visit change. (Source: RANZCP Mood CPG)

options.text: Refer urgently to nephrology for consideration of renal biopsy before making any change to lithium therapy at this level of function
options.rationale: Biopsy is not routinely indicated for typical lithium nephropathy (chronic tubulointerstitial pattern); nephrology referral is appropriate for co-management but does not obviate the need to adjust lithium now. (Source: KHA-CARI; Australian Prescriber)

options.text: Switch perindopril to amlodipine on the basis that ACE inhibitors are contributing to falling eGFR and lithium can then be continued unchanged safely
options.rationale: ACEi may be a contributor but stopping it does not address cumulative lithium tubulointerstitial injury; the primary issue is lithium exposure, not the antihypertensive class. (Source: KHA-CARI; TG Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Chronic lithium nephropathy is a slowly progressive tubulointerstitial injury. Continued use is often justified when the psychiatric benefit is clear, but the target level should be lowered, monitoring intensified, and a multidisciplinary discussion held about long-term trajectory.
key_points: Target 0.4-0.6 mmol/L in older adults or CKD
3-monthly levels once monitoring becomes intensive
Abrupt cessation carries a 50% relapse risk within 6 months
Switch requires slow cross-titration under psychiatry review
explanation.pearls: In context: never stop lithium at a single GP visit; adjust and involve the treating team.

stem:
A 36-year-old man on clozapine 400 mg nocte for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (18 months, stable) has a routine weekly FBC as part of the CPMS/ClopineCentral monitoring program. He is well, denies fever or infection, and has no other medication changes. The FBC returns while he is still in the clinic waiting room and the nurse escalates it to you.

He has no personal or family history of haematological disorders and does not identify as being of a background with a high prevalence of benign ethnic neutropenia.

data_table.Examination: Well, no oral ulcers, no lymphadenopathy, no signs of infection.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 3.1 x10^9/L, absolute neutrophil count (ANC) 1.2 x10^9/L, Hb 142 g/L, platelets 240 x10^9/L. Previous ANC 2.3 four weeks ago.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately, admit for reverse isolation and commence broad-spectrum antibiotics with G-CSF while awaiting haematology review
options.rationale: This is amber-range (not red), and cessation is not required at ANC 1.2; premature stopping risks psychiatric relapse and rechallenge is often refused. Empirical antibiotics and G-CSF are for febrile neutropenia or ANC <0.5. (Source: TGA clozapine PI; CPMS)

options.text: Continue clozapine unchanged and repeat FBC at the routine four-weekly interval since he is asymptomatic and there is no other red flag
options.rationale: An ANC of 1.2 shifts him from green to amber under the Australian CPMS/ClopineCentral protocol; monitoring must escalate to at least twice-weekly FBCs, not remain at the routine interval. (Source: CPMS/ClopineCentral)

options.text: Cease clozapine and switch to olanzapine 20 mg nocte as an equivalent-efficacy alternative pending haematology review of the neutropenia today
options.rationale: Olanzapine is not equivalent for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (clozapine is uniquely effective); switching at amber range is premature and loses the only agent with demonstrated benefit in this indication. (Source: RANZCP CPG Schizophrenia)

options.text: Continue clozapine, increase FBC monitoring to twice-weekly until ANC returns to green range (>=2.0), and educate the patient on infection red flags
options.rationale: Under the Australian clozapine monitoring protocol, ANC 1.0-1.5 is amber: continue clozapine but escalate to twice-weekly FBCs until ANC returns to >=2.0. Cessation is only required at red-range (ANC <1.0). Patient education on infection is essential. (Source: CPMS/ClopineCentral protocol; TGA clozapine PI)

options.text: Continue clozapine but reduce the dose to 200 mg nocte on the basis that neutropenia is a dose-dependent adverse effect that reverses with dose reduction
options.rationale: Clozapine-induced neutropenia is idiosyncratic, not dose-dependent; dose reduction does not resolve it and may destabilise psychiatric state. (Source: TGA clozapine PI)

explanation.summary: Australian clozapine monitoring (CPMS or ClopineCentral) uses a traffic-light system based on ANC. Green (>=2.0) is routine, amber (1.0-1.9 depending on protocol) requires increased monitoring, red (<1.0) requires cessation.
key_points: Green ANC >=2.0: routine monitoring
Amber ANC 1.0-1.9: increase to twice-weekly, continue clozapine
Red ANC <1.0: cease clozapine, notify haematology
G-CSF is used in some rechallenge or persistent red-range cases with haematology guidance
explanation.pearls: In context: know the traffic-light thresholds cold; ANC 1.2 is amber, not red.

subtopic_detail: First 6-8 week troponin and CRP screening
stem:
A 24-year-old man was commenced on clozapine 21 days ago for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, titrated to 200 mg nocte. He presents with 48 hours of low-grade fever, mild dyspnoea and pleuritic chest pain. He is otherwise stable and his mental state has improved on clozapine.

His routine baseline monitoring included ECG, echocardiogram, troponin and CRP, all normal. He has no personal or family history of cardiac disease and no recent viral illness in the household.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 108/64, RR 22, SpO2 96% on air, temp 37.9.
data_table.Examination: Mildly dyspnoeic, no murmur, no pericardial rub, chest clear.
data_table.Investigations: Troponin I 62 ng/L (upper reference 26), CRP 84 mg/L, ECG sinus tachycardia with non-specific T wave flattening, FBC normal, ANC 3.8.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine, admit for cardiology review including urgent echocardiogram, and do not rechallenge without specialist input, cardiology review
options.rationale: Rising troponin plus CRP with tachycardia and dyspnoea 3 weeks into clozapine is myocarditis until proven otherwise; TGA PI and RANZCP guidance require cessation, cardiology involvement and echo. Rechallenge is possible in selected cases but only under specialist care. (Source: TGA clozapine PI; RANZCP)

options.text: Continue clozapine at current dose, prescribe paracetamol for fever, and recheck troponin and CRP in 48 hours before making a management decision
options.rationale: Continuing clozapine with clear biochemical and clinical signs of myocarditis risks fulminant progression; delay in cessation is associated with worse outcome including death. (Source: TGA clozapine PI)

options.text: Continue clozapine and start empirical oral doxycycline 100 mg bd for a presumed atypical respiratory infection given the fever, dyspnoea and tachycardia
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics without infective focus do not address clozapine myocarditis and the antibiotic choice does not treat the underlying cardiac process; myocarditis mortality is highest in the first 6-8 weeks. (Source: TG Antibiotic; TGA PI)

options.text: Reduce clozapine to 100 mg nocte, continue slow titration schedule at halved rate, and repeat troponin weekly while remaining as an outpatient in community
options.rationale: Dose reduction does not adequately mitigate the risk of established myocarditis and outpatient management is unsafe with an elevated troponin and tachycardia. (Source: TGA clozapine PI)

options.text: Continue clozapine and refer for outpatient cardiac MRI within four weeks to confirm myocarditis before making any changes to psychiatric medication
options.rationale: A 4-week wait for MRI while continuing clozapine risks progression to fulminant myocarditis; cessation and urgent echo are required now, with MRI as an adjunct if diagnosis remains uncertain. (Source: Australian Prescriber; TGA PI)

explanation.summary: Clozapine myocarditis peaks between weeks 2 and 4 of initiation. Australian practice is baseline troponin/CRP/ECG/echo, then weekly troponin and CRP for the first 4 (some centres 6-8) weeks. Any rise triggers cessation and cardiology review.
key_points: Peak incidence weeks 2-4 of clozapine initiation
Weekly troponin and CRP for at least 4 weeks (many centres 6-8 weeks)
Cease clozapine if troponin or CRP rise with symptoms
Rechallenge only under specialist cardiology and psychiatry co-supervision
explanation.pearls: In context: fever, tachycardia and dyspnoea in the first 8 weeks of clozapine is myocarditis until proven otherwise.

subtopic_detail: Highest-mortality side effect and aperient prophylaxis
stem:
A 48-year-old woman on clozapine 500 mg nocte for eight years presents to ED with three days of increasing abdominal distension, nausea and no bowel motion for six days. She admits to chronic constipation, uses lactulose intermittently but has been non-adherent for two weeks. She has no fever.

She is otherwise medically well, does not use opioids, and has no prior abdominal surgery.

data_table.Examination: Grossly distended, tympanic, minimal bowel sounds, mild diffuse tenderness, no peritonism, empty rectum.
data_table.Investigations: AXR gross faecal loading throughout colon with dilated loops (transverse colon 8 cm), CT confirms severe constipation with early small bowel dilatation, no perforation, lactate 2.1.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue clozapine, prescribe oral macrogol at usual dose and discharge with GP follow-up for further titration of laxative therapy over the next week
options.rationale: Discharge is unsafe given tympanic distension, tachycardia, elevated lactate and early small bowel dilatation; clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) has a mortality up to 15-27% once complications develop. (Source: Australian Prescriber; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe metoclopramide 10 mg IV three times daily as a prokinetic and monitor for symptomatic improvement over the next 12 hours before considering imaging
options.rationale: Metoclopramide primarily accelerates upper GI transit and adds extrapyramidal and tardive dyskinesia risk on top of clozapine; it does not reliably resolve colonic hypomotility. (Source: AMH: Metoclopramide)

options.text: Perform a manual disimpaction in the ED and arrange same-day outpatient colonoscopy for evaluation of possible mechanical obstruction contributing to the picture
options.rationale: Disimpaction alone is inadequate for whole-colon faecal loading with proximal dilatation; same-day colonoscopy carries perforation risk in a distended obstructed bowel. Surgical review and admission are required. (Source: Australian Prescriber)

options.text: Admit, keep nil by mouth with IV fluids, involve surgery, cease clozapine and start multi-agent aperients with serial abdominal examination, review after 48 h
options.rationale: Established clozapine ileus needs admission, fluid resuscitation, surgical involvement (risk of ischaemia or perforation), temporary cessation of clozapine and multi-agent aperient regimen (osmotic plus stimulant). This is the highest-mortality clozapine adverse effect, exceeding agranulocytosis. (Source: Australian Prescriber; TGA PI)

options.text: Continue clozapine, prescribe a sodium picosulfate bowel preparation regimen and arrange outpatient colonic transit study in the next fortnight for further work up
options.rationale: Aggressive bowel prep in a distended, dilated colon risks perforation; outpatient investigation delays management of a potentially fatal complication. (Source: Australian Prescriber)

explanation.summary: Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility (CIGH) is the highest-mortality clozapine adverse effect, exceeding agranulocytosis. All patients on clozapine should be on scheduled aperient prophylaxis (typically macrogol +/- stimulant), and any established constipation is a medical emergency.
key_points: CIGH mortality up to 15-27% once complicated
Prophylactic aperient (macrogol +/- senna) for all clozapine patients
Established ileus: admit, IV fluids, surgical review, cease clozapine
Avoid opioids and additional anticholinergic drugs on clozapine
explanation.pearls: In context: constipation on clozapine is not a nuisance, it is the biggest killer.

subtopic_detail: Impact of smoking cessation on plasma levels
stem:
A 40-year-old man on clozapine 450 mg nocte for schizophrenia (5 years, stable) is admitted to a medical ward for cellulitis. He is a smoker of 30 cigarettes/day. On day two of admission he tells you he has been given nicotine patches and has not smoked since arrival. On day four he develops sedation, hypersalivation, mild myoclonus and a resting tremor.

He is afebrile, no infective deterioration, and no new medications have been started other than IV flucloxacillin.

data_table.Examination: Sedated but rousable, hypersalivation, fine tremor, hyperreflexia mild.
data_table.Investigations: Clozapine level 1180 microg/L (pre-admission 620), norclozapine 340, FBC and CRP unchanged from admission, ECG QTc 460 ms.

lead_in: What is the most likely mechanism and best immediate action?

options.text: Clozapine level has risen because of loss of tobacco induction of CYP1A2; reduce clozapine dose and monitor level and clinical response daily, support cessation
options.rationale: Tobacco smoke (polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, not nicotine) induces CYP1A2, the principal enzyme metabolising clozapine. Cessation removes induction and levels can rise 50-100% within 2-4 weeks (faster on inpatient wards). Dose reduction of ~25% is often required within days. (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH)
source_refs: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

options.text: Nicotine replacement patches have precipitated clozapine toxicity via a direct pharmacokinetic interaction at the CYP1A2 enzyme system similar to tobacco itself
options.rationale: Nicotine itself does not induce CYP1A2; the inducers are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke, so NRT does not maintain enzyme induction after cessation. This is a common misconception. (Source: Australian Prescriber)
source_refs: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

options.text: Flucloxacillin has inhibited hepatic clozapine metabolism producing an acute toxic rise in plasma level that should resolve on completion of the antibiotic course
options.rationale: Flucloxacillin has no clinically significant effect on CYP1A2 or clozapine levels; the mechanism here is loss of tobacco induction, not antibiotic inhibition. (Source: AMH interactions)

options.text: The clozapine assay is spuriously elevated by sampling outside the recommended trough window and the true steady-state level is unchanged from baseline
options.rationale: A near-doubling of level with new toxic symptoms cannot be explained by sampling timing alone; the pattern is classic for smoking cessation. (Source: TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Cellulitis-related inflammation reduces hepatic clozapine clearance transiently; recheck level in 48 hours before making any dose change to therapy
options.rationale: Acute inflammation can raise clozapine levels somewhat but the dominant driver here is smoking cessation; withholding dose action for another 48 hours risks clinical deterioration when the patient is already toxic. (Source: Australian Prescriber)
source_refs: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

explanation.summary: Tobacco (not nicotine) induces CYP1A2. Any smoking cessation, hospital admission with enforced abstinence, or planned quit attempt is a trigger for pre-emptive clozapine dose review. Levels can rise substantially within days to weeks.
key_points: Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco induce CYP1A2, not nicotine
Cessation can raise clozapine levels 50-100% within 2-4 weeks
Consider 25% dose reduction on planned or enforced cessation
Restart smoking during admission is not the answer; adjust dose
explanation.pearls: In context: any clozapine patient who stops smoking needs a dose plan, not just a patch.

sources.label: Australian Prescriber: Smoking and drug interactions

subtopic_detail: TGA restrictions and pregnancy prevention program
stem:
A 27-year-old woman with bipolar I disorder is stable on sodium valproate 1 g bd (18 months, no relapses). She attends for review and reports that she has recently started a new relationship and wants to stop contraception in the next 6 months to attempt pregnancy. Previous trials of lithium (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus) and lamotrigine (SJS) both failed.

She understands the diagnosis, has capacity, and has read written materials about her medication.

data_table.Examination: Well, no adverse effects on current dose.
data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, ammonia normal, valproate level 480 micromol/L, contraception: combined oral contraceptive current, no recent pregnancy tests.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue valproate, recommend high-dose folate 5 mg daily and cease contraception in six months as her mood is stable and folate reduces neural tube defect risk sufficiently for planned pregnancy
options.rationale: Folate does not mitigate the specific teratogenic and neurodevelopmental risks of valproate; TGA prescribing information requires pregnancy prevention while on valproate in women of childbearing potential unless there is no alternative and the program is followed. (Source: TGA valproate PI)

options.text: Enrol her in the valproate pregnancy prevention program, arrange psychiatry review to explore alternatives, and continue contraception during transition, contraception documented
options.rationale: TGA/AMH mandate valproate is not used in women of childbearing potential unless there is no effective alternative, and only under the pregnancy prevention program (annual specialist review, effective contraception, acknowledgement of risks). Alternatives must be actively considered before pregnancy planning. (Source: TGA; AMH; RANZCP)

options.text: Halve the valproate dose to 500 mg bd immediately and check level at trough; a lower dose reduces teratogenic risk to an acceptable range for planned pregnancy and preserves clinical stability
options.rationale: Dose reduction below a threshold does not remove teratogenic risk (dose-response is present but no safe threshold); also risks psychiatric relapse. Not a substitute for switching. (Source: TGA valproate PI)

options.text: Cease valproate today, commence quetiapine 300 mg nocte and advise pregnancy attempts can start immediately provided ongoing psychiatric follow up is maintained across the plan
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of valproate risks relapse; any switch requires cross-titration under psychiatry, and pregnancy planning should follow stability on the new agent, not commence immediately. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for pre-implantation genetic testing so the couple can screen embryos for valproate-related neural tube defects prior to implantation and continue valproate in pregnancy
options.rationale: Valproate-associated malformations and neurodevelopmental problems are not detectable by preimplantation genetic testing; this is not an appropriate substitute for medication review. (Source: TGA valproate PI)

explanation.summary: Valproate carries the highest teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental risk of any commonly used mood stabiliser (up to 30-40% neurodevelopmental disorders, ~10% major malformations). The TGA-mandated Australian pregnancy prevention program requires effective contraception, annual specialist review and documented risk acknowledgement.
key_points: Neurodevelopmental disorder risk 30-40%, malformation risk ~10%
Pregnancy prevention program mandatory in women of childbearing potential
Folate does not mitigate valproate teratogenicity
No safe threshold dose in pregnancy
explanation.pearls: In context: never plan pregnancy on valproate; switch first, then attempt.

stem:
A 32-year-old woman of Han Chinese background is being considered for carbamazepine as second-line mood stabiliser after inadequate response to lithium (nephrotoxicity concerns) and intolerance of valproate (severe weight gain). She has no personal or family history of skin reactions to medications and is currently on no other drugs.

She has capacity, understands the diagnosis and has agreed to shared decision-making regarding options.

data_table.Investigations: FBC, LFTs and UEC normal. Sodium 140, no baseline pharmacogenomic testing yet performed.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before commencing carbamazepine?

options.text: Perform HLA-B*15:02 genotyping and only proceed with carbamazepine if she tests negative for the allele; positive result mandates avoidance of the drug, involve neurology and pharmacy
options.rationale: TGA product information and eviQ pharmacogenomic guidance recommend HLA-B*15:02 testing before carbamazepine (and oxcarbazepine) in individuals of Han Chinese, Thai, Malay, Filipino, Indian and some other Asian ancestries due to strong association with SJS/TEN. Positive result is a contraindication. (Source: TGA carbamazepine PI; eviQ)

options.text: Commence carbamazepine at standard low starting dose with slow titration and counsel her to present immediately if any rash appears during the first eight weeks of therapy
options.rationale: Rash counselling alone is insufficient when a validated screening test with high negative predictive value is available; testing is now standard of care in populations with high HLA-B*15:02 prevalence. (Source: TGA; eviQ)

options.text: Substitute oxcarbazepine for carbamazepine as it is chemically similar but does not carry any risk of SJS/TEN or the HLA-B*15:02 pharmacogenomic association in Asian populations
options.rationale: Oxcarbazepine shares the HLA-B*15:02 association with SJS/TEN, though at lower absolute risk; substitution does not remove the need for screening. (Source: TGA oxcarbazepine PI)

options.text: Perform HLA-B*57:01 testing before commencing carbamazepine as this allele confers major hypersensitivity risk to aromatic anticonvulsants across all patient populations in Australia
options.rationale: HLA-B*57:01 is the abacavir hypersensitivity marker, not carbamazepine SJS/TEN. The relevant allele is HLA-B*15:02 for carbamazepine SJS/TEN in Asian populations and HLA-A*31:01 for other reactions. (Source: eviQ)

options.text: Proceed with carbamazepine at a slow titration schedule and check LFTs weekly for four weeks as the main serious risk is hepatotoxicity rather than severe cutaneous adverse reaction
options.rationale: Hepatotoxicity and haematological effects require monitoring but the highest-consequence pharmacogenomic risk in this ancestry group is SJS/TEN; screening is the appropriate first step, not routine LFT surveillance alone. (Source: TGA carbamazepine PI)

explanation.summary: HLA-B*15:02 is strongly associated with carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN in Han Chinese, Thai, Malay, Filipino, Indian, Vietnamese and some other Asian populations. TGA now recommends screening before initiation.
key_points: HLA-B*15:02 -> carbamazepine SJS/TEN in Asian populations
HLA-A*31:01 -> broader hypersensitivity reactions
Oxcarbazepine also carries the HLA-B*15:02 association at lower risk
Screening and avoidance in positives is standard of care
explanation.pearls: In context: never start carbamazepine in an at-risk ancestry without checking HLA-B*15:02.

subtopic_detail: Titration with valproate co-therapy and COC interaction
stem:
A 29-year-old woman with bipolar II disorder is stabilised on sodium valproate 500 mg bd. Her psychiatrist decides to add lamotrigine for a predominantly depressive relapse pattern. She is also on a combined oral contraceptive pill and has no history of rash.

She is otherwise well and takes no other medications.

data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, valproate level 460 micromol/L, FBC normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate lamotrigine starting and titration approach?

options.text: Standard lamotrigine titration starting at 25 mg daily with weekly doubling to 100 mg over four weeks; the COC has no effect on lamotrigine metabolism in this age group
options.rationale: Standard titration is too fast when valproate (a potent lamotrigine metabolism inhibitor) is co-prescribed; risk of SJS/TEN rises with rapid escalation. COC induces lamotrigine glucuronidation and reduces levels. (Source: AMH: Lamotrigine)

options.text: Load lamotrigine at 200 mg on day one to achieve rapid therapeutic effect; this approach is preferred in bipolar depression where symptom burden is high and time to effect matters
options.rationale: Loading doses are contraindicated for lamotrigine at any indication because of SJS/TEN risk; slow titration is essential regardless of urgency. (Source: TGA lamotrigine PI)

options.text: Cease valproate before starting lamotrigine and then use standard monotherapy titration since combining the two agents provides no clinical benefit in bipolar spectrum illness overall
options.rationale: Combination of lamotrigine and valproate is a recognised strategy; abrupt cessation of valproate risks relapse and is not required, provided titration is appropriately slow. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Start lamotrigine 25 mg on alternate days for two weeks, then 25 mg daily for two weeks, then increase by 25-50 mg every two weeks under review, review at each dose step
options.rationale: Valproate roughly doubles lamotrigine levels via UGT inhibition, so start at 25 mg on alternate days for weeks 1-2, 25 mg daily weeks 3-4, then increase by 25-50 mg every 2 weeks. Standard titration risks SJS/TEN. COC induces lamotrigine metabolism and dose review is needed when COC starts or stops. (Source: AMH; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise stopping the COC before commencing lamotrigine as they are contraindicated together; use a copper intrauterine device from cycle day one for ongoing contraception plan
options.rationale: COC and lamotrigine can be co-prescribed but the interaction (COC induces lamotrigine metabolism) requires dose review when COC starts or stops; they are not contraindicated together. (Source: AMH: Lamotrigine)

explanation.summary: Lamotrigine SJS/TEN risk is highest with rapid titration or overshoot dosing. Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation (levels roughly double), so halve the starting dose and slow the titration. COC induces lamotrigine glucuronidation, so dose adjustment is required when COC is started or stopped.
key_points: Valproate co-therapy: start 25 mg alternate days, halve steady state dose
COC: induces lamotrigine glucuronidation; adjust dose on starting/stopping
Any rash within first 8 weeks: cease and reassess
No loading doses at any indication
explanation.pearls: In context: lamotrigine + valproate = slow titration; lamotrigine + COC = watch for level changes.

subtopic_detail: Switching from MAOI to SSRI with safe washout period
stem:
A 52-year-old woman with treatment-resistant atypical depression has been on phenelzine 45 mg daily for 10 months with partial response. Ongoing symptoms lead her psychiatrist to plan a switch to sertraline. She asks how the transition will be managed and what she needs to do at home.

She has been adherent to a low-tyramine diet and has no significant medical comorbidities.

data_table.Investigations: LFTs normal, ECG normal, UEC normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate transition plan?

options.text: Cease phenelzine today, wait 14 days off all MAOI medication (with dietary restrictions continuing during this washout), then commence sertraline at usual starting dose, with handover
options.rationale: TGA product information and TG Psychotropic require at least 14 days off an irreversible non-selective MAOI (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) before commencing an SSRI, SNRI or other serotonergic drug, to allow regeneration of monoamine oxidase enzyme. Tyramine dietary restriction should continue for the full washout. (Source: TG Psychotropic; TGA phenelzine PI)

options.text: Cross-titrate by reducing phenelzine and introducing sertraline in overlapping doses over two weeks to minimise the depressive symptom gap that occurs during a strict washout period
options.rationale: Cross-titration of an irreversible MAOI and an SSRI is contraindicated because of the risk of fatal serotonin syndrome; overlap must be avoided. (Source: TG Psychotropic; TGA)

options.text: Cease phenelzine and start sertraline after a 5-day washout as this is sufficient given phenelzine's short elimination half-life of approximately 12 hours from the last dose administered
options.rationale: Phenelzine is an irreversible MAOI; despite short plasma half-life, MAO enzyme regeneration requires ~14 days. Elimination half-life is not the relevant kinetic parameter. (Source: TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease phenelzine and start moclobemide (a reversible MAOI-A) after a 24-hour washout as an interim step, then transition to sertraline after a further two weeks in the sequence
options.rationale: Switching one MAOI class to another does not remove the SSRI overlap risk; the required 14-day washout applies before any SSRI regardless of intermediate agents. (Source: TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease phenelzine and start sertraline after a 48-hour washout given adequate dietary washout and absence of any drug interactions with other medications she is currently taking at home
options.rationale: 48 hours is grossly insufficient for irreversible MAOI enzyme regeneration; risk of serotonin syndrome remains high. (Source: TGA phenelzine PI)

explanation.summary: Irreversible MAOIs (phenelzine, tranylcypromine) require a 14-day washout before starting any serotonergic drug (SSRI, SNRI, TCA, opioids like tramadol/pethidine, triptans). Fluoxetine to MAOI switch requires a 5-week washout due to fluoxetine's long half-life.
key_points: 14-day washout after phenelzine or tranylcypromine before SSRI
5-week washout after fluoxetine before MAOI
Continue tyramine restriction throughout MAOI washout
Never cross-titrate irreversible MAOI with serotonergic agent
explanation.pearls: In context: 14 days off MAOI, 5 weeks off fluoxetine, always.

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing serotonin syndrome, NMS, anticholinergic and linezolid interactions
stem:
A 46-year-old man with major depressive disorder on venlafaxine 225 mg daily is admitted from ED with confusion, agitation, sweating, dilated pupils, tremor and myoclonus. Vitals show HR 128, BP 168/102, RR 24, temperature 39.1. He was commenced on linezolid IV three days ago for MRSA vertebral osteomyelitis. On examination he has hyperreflexia and inducible clonus, particularly in the lower limbs. Mental state is agitated but not rigid.

He has no recent antipsychotic exposure.

data_table.Examination: Dilated pupils, sweating, hyperreflexia, sustained clonus L>R, coarse tremor, agitation.
data_table.Investigations: CK 340 U/L (mildly elevated), UEC and LFTs normal, no leukocytosis.

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis and best immediate action?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome; commence dantrolene, cease all serotonergic agents and support in ICU with cooling and rehydration measures throughout resuscitation
options.rationale: NMS features bradyreflexia and lead-pipe rigidity, not hyperreflexia and clonus; also requires antipsychotic exposure. Clinical pattern here is serotonin syndrome. (Source: TG Psychotropic; Australian Prescriber)
source_refs: TG Psychotropic: Serotonin syndrome vs NMS

options.text: Anticholinergic toxidrome from an occult ingestion; commence physostigmine as reversal agent, admit for cardiac monitoring and psychiatric review after clinical stabilisation is achieved
options.rationale: Anticholinergic toxidrome has flushed dry skin, absent bowel sounds and urinary retention, without hyperreflexia or clonus. Sweating in this patient argues against anticholinergic aetiology. (Source: TG Toxicology)

options.text: Serotonin syndrome from venlafaxine-linezolid interaction; cease both serotonergic agents, supportive care with benzodiazepines, cooling, cyproheptadine if severe, admit to a monitored bed
options.rationale: Linezolid is a reversible weak MAOI and combined with venlafaxine (SNRI) can precipitate serotonin syndrome. Hyperreflexia, sustained clonus (particularly lower limb), mydriasis, sweating, agitation and hyperthermia meet Hunter criteria. Cease serotonergic drugs, aggressive supportive care, IV benzodiazepines. Cyproheptadine (5HT2A antagonist) for severe/refractory cases. (Source: TG Psychotropic; PIC 13 11 26)

options.text: Malignant hyperthermia triggered by recent anaesthetic exposure; commence dantrolene infusion, active cooling and admission to high dependency unit for close monitoring of temperature and CK
options.rationale: Malignant hyperthermia requires exposure to a triggering anaesthetic (volatile agent or succinylcholine); the patient has had no such exposure. Presentation is otherwise consistent with serotonin syndrome. (Source: ANZCA)

options.text: Sepsis with metabolic encephalopathy from progression of the osteomyelitis; commence broad-spectrum antibiotics escalation, source control review and empirical steroids for suspected relative adrenal insufficiency
options.rationale: Sepsis does not cause sustained clonus and hyperreflexia; the pattern here is serotonergic toxicity, not sepsis progression, and steroids are not indicated. (Source: TG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Serotonin syndrome and NMS both cause hyperthermia and autonomic instability, but neuromuscular signs distinguish them: hyperreflexia and clonus (SS) vs rigidity and bradyreflexia (NMS). Anticholinergic toxidrome is dry and flushed. Linezolid is a reversible MAOI and a common precipitant of SS when combined with serotonergic antidepressants.
key_points: Hunter criteria: clonus + serotonergic exposure + one of agitation, hyperreflexia, autonomic instability
Linezolid is a reversible MAOI - avoid or cease serotonergic agents
Cease drug, benzodiazepines, active cooling; cyproheptadine for severe cases
NMS: rigidity, bradyreflexia, high CK; anticholinergic: dry, flushed, absent bowel sounds
explanation.pearls: In context: hyperreflexia and clonus with autonomic storm = serotonin syndrome; rigidity + antipsychotic exposure = NMS.

stem:
A 34-year-old woman is brought to ED 90 minutes after ingesting an unknown quantity of amitriptyline in a suicide attempt. She is drowsy, confused, warm and flushed. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 128, PR normal, QRS 128 ms, terminal R wave in aVR, QTc 480 ms. BP is 88/50. She has had one brief generalised seizure in triage that self-terminated within 30 seconds.

She is intubated for airway protection and started on IV crystalloid.

data_table.Examination: GCS 8 pre-intubation, dilated pupils, dry skin, hyperreflexia.
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 128 ms, terminal R wave aVR, VBG pH 7.28, sodium 138, potassium 3.6, lactate 3.4, paracetamol level pending.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Administer intravenous flumazenil to reverse the sedation and improve airway protection before making further decisions about ongoing airway or ventilation management strategy
options.rationale: Flumazenil is contraindicated in TCA overdose (may lower seizure threshold and unmask arrhythmia); it does not address sodium channel blockade. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)

options.text: Administer intravenous lidocaine (lignocaine) infusion as class Ib antiarrhythmic to reverse the ventricular ectopy and QRS prolongation seen on the current bedside ECG tracing
options.rationale: Class Ia and Ic antiarrhythmics are contraindicated (worsen sodium channel blockade); lidocaine (class Ib) is second line if bicarbonate fails but not first line. Bicarbonate is the primary intervention. (Source: TG Toxicology)

options.text: Give IV magnesium sulfate 2 g as initial treatment for the widened QRS and associated risk of torsades de pointes in TCA overdose with concurrent QTc prolongation on presentation ECG
options.rationale: Magnesium has a role for TCA-associated arrhythmias but is not the first-line therapy for QRS widening; sodium bicarbonate is. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)

options.text: Start intralipid 20% emulsion infusion as first-line treatment for lipophilic TCA toxicity in the setting of QRS prolongation, hypotension and post-seizure state after suicide attempt
options.rationale: Intralipid is a rescue therapy for severe cardiotoxicity unresponsive to sodium bicarbonate; not first-line for TCA overdose. (Source: PIC 13 11 26)

options.text: Administer IV sodium bicarbonate bolus (1-2 mmol/kg) to narrow the QRS and raise blood pressure, and repeat as needed with electrolyte monitoring, with airway support
options.rationale: TCA cardiotoxicity is driven by fast sodium channel blockade; sodium bicarbonate (1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus) reverses the block by both sodium loading and alkalinisation, aiming to narrow QRS below 100 ms. Also indicated for TCA-associated hypotension and ventricular arrhythmia. (Source: TG Toxicology; PIC 13 11 26)

explanation.summary: TCA cardiotoxicity is fast-sodium-channel-blockade-driven. QRS >100 ms predicts seizures, QRS >160 ms predicts ventricular arrhythmia. Sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg IV bolus is first-line, repeated to narrow QRS <100 ms and support blood pressure.
key_points: QRS >100 ms: give sodium bicarbonate
Terminal R wave aVR >3 mm is a supportive marker
Avoid flumazenil, class Ia/Ic antiarrhythmics, physostigmine
Intralipid is rescue for refractory cardiotoxicity
explanation.pearls: In context: any TCA overdose with QRS >100 ms gets bicarbonate.

stem:
A 38-year-old woman on paroxetine 20 mg daily for 18 months attends her GP asking to stop the medication. Her depression has been in full remission for over 12 months and she is well-supported. She reports missing occasional doses when travelling and feeling flu-like and dizzy within 24 hours.

She has no other medications and no significant comorbidities.

data_table.Examination: Well, no depressive symptoms on MSE.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate discontinuation plan?

options.text: Cease paroxetine today and provide brief education about self-limiting flu-like symptoms that may occur over the first fortnight after stopping the medication in general practice
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation of paroxetine (a short half-life SSRI with strong discontinuation profile) commonly causes distressing discontinuation symptoms; gradual taper is standard. (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH)

options.text: Switch to a long half-life SSRI such as fluoxetine 20 mg for two weeks and then abruptly stop; this avoids the taper process altogether and eliminates discontinuation symptoms
options.rationale: Cross-taper via fluoxetine can be used for difficult cases but is not first line; a paroxetine taper is usually sufficient and simpler for the patient. (Source: TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue paroxetine indefinitely because the flu-like symptoms during missed doses indicate that the patient remains dependent on the medication for continued mood stability
options.rationale: Discontinuation symptoms on missed doses are pharmacological, not evidence of dependence or need for continued treatment; recurrence risk is a separate consideration. (Source: Australian Prescriber)

options.text: Halve to paroxetine 10 mg daily this week and cease completely the following week; a rapid two-week taper minimises total exposure and avoids prolonged withdrawal effects over time
options.rationale: A 2-week rapid taper is often too fast for paroxetine and provokes marked discontinuation symptoms; a longer taper (typically 4+ weeks) is standard. (Source: TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Taper paroxetine over several weeks (halve to 10 mg for 2-4 weeks, then 10 mg alternate days, then cease), monitoring for discontinuation and relapse, with review at each step
options.rationale: Paroxetine has a short half-life (~24 h) and strong discontinuation syndrome; gradual taper over weeks reduces symptoms. Discontinuation vs relapse can be distinguished by timing (discontinuation within days, self-limiting) and symptom pattern (flu-like, dizziness, electric shock sensations). (Source: TG Psychotropic; AMH)

explanation.summary: Discontinuation syndrome is most marked with short half-life antidepressants (paroxetine, venlafaxine). Symptoms include flu-like features, dizziness, electric shock sensations, insomnia and irritability, typically within days of dose reduction, and are self-limiting.
key_points: Paroxetine and venlafaxine have the strongest discontinuation profile
Distinguish discontinuation (days, self-limiting, flu-like) from relapse (weeks, sustained low mood)
Fluoxetine cross-taper is a rescue strategy for difficult tapers
Slow taper over at least 4 weeks (often longer) is standard
explanation.pearls: In context: never stop paroxetine abruptly; taper over weeks.

subtopic_detail: Switch strategy for symptomatic prolactin elevation
stem:
A 28-year-old woman with schizophrenia stabilised on risperidone 4 mg daily for 12 months presents with amenorrhoea for 6 months, galactorrhoea and loss of libido. Pregnancy is excluded. Prolactin is 2400 mIU/L (upper reference 500). TSH and pituitary MRI are normal.

She is otherwise well, denies mood symptoms, and does not want to become pregnant in the immediate future.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral galactorrhoea, no visual field defect.
data_table.Investigations: Prolactin 2400 mIU/L, TSH 1.8, MRI pituitary normal, beta-hCG negative.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step?

options.text: Continue risperidone and add cabergoline 0.5 mg twice weekly to lower prolactin, with monitoring for possible psychiatric destabilisation from dopamine agonist therapy over the following months
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists can precipitate psychotic relapse in schizophrenia and are not first line for antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia; switching antipsychotic is preferred. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Continue risperidone and reassure her that antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia does not cause long-term consequences and menstruation typically returns once psychiatric symptoms fully remit
options.rationale: Sustained hyperprolactinaemia is associated with hypogonadism, reduced bone mineral density and infertility; it warrants intervention when symptomatic. (Source: Australian Prescriber)

options.text: Cease risperidone abruptly and commence olanzapine 20 mg nocte as it does not cause hyperprolactinaemia; this can be done as a same-day switch without any cross-titration for convenience
options.rationale: Olanzapine causes mild-moderate prolactin elevation (less than risperidone but not neutral); abrupt switch risks psychiatric destabilisation. Aripiprazole is the more reliable prolactin-lowering choice. (Source: TG Psychotropic; RANZCP)

options.text: Cross-titrate to aripiprazole (a partial dopamine D2 agonist) which lowers prolactin, with a gradual switch over several weeks under psychiatric supervision, and monitor prolactin at 6 weeks
options.rationale: Aripiprazole is a partial D2 agonist and consistently lowers prolactin; it is the preferred switch or adjunct in antipsychotic-induced hyperprolactinaemia with clinical impact. Cross-titration under psychiatric supervision preserves efficacy while addressing prolactin. (Source: RANZCP; TG Psychotropic)

options.text: Halve the risperidone dose to 2 mg daily and reassess prolactin at eight weeks; if prolactin remains elevated then consider dopamine agonist addition to further reduce the level over time
options.rationale: Dose reduction may modestly reduce prolactin but risks loss of efficacy and does not reliably resolve symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia; switch to aripiprazole is preferred. (Source: RANZCP)

explanation.summary: Risperidone, amisulpride and paliperidone are the most prolactin-elevating antipsychotics. Aripiprazole (partial D2 agonist) is the reliable low-prolactin choice and can be used as switch or adjunct to lower prolactin. Cabergoline risks psychiatric destabilisation in schizophrenia.
key_points: High-prolactin: risperidone, paliperidone, amisulpride, haloperidol
Low-prolactin: aripiprazole, quetiapine
Symptomatic hyperprolactinaemia: switch to aripiprazole preferred
Avoid dopamine agonists in schizophrenia unless specialist-guided
explanation.pearls: In context: symptomatic prolactin rise on risperidone -> aripiprazole switch.

subtopic_detail: Oral to long-acting injectable transition with overlap
stem:
A 35-year-old man with schizophrenia stable on oral paliperidone 6 mg daily for 8 months is being switched to paliperidone palmitate long-acting injectable due to recurrent adherence problems. He has tolerated oral paliperidone well and has no cardiac or renal issues. He agrees to depot therapy after shared decision-making.

His current adherence is estimated at 60% and previous relapses have followed medication cessation.

data_table.Examination: Well, no adverse effects on oral paliperidone.
data_table.Investigations: UEC, LFTs, FBC normal, ECG normal, no other medications.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initiation regimen for paliperidone palmitate?

options.text: Give paliperidone palmitate 100 mg IM gluteal monthly starting today and continue oral paliperidone 6 mg daily for 4 weeks to ensure adequate therapeutic coverage during the induction phase
options.rationale: Standard paliperidone palmitate initiation uses deltoid (not gluteal) loading with the specific 150/100 mg two-dose regimen; oral overlap is not required if the loading is followed. Also, monthly monotherapy without loading gives sub-therapeutic levels initially. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI)

options.text: Cease oral paliperidone and start haloperidol decanoate 100 mg IM monthly as a cheaper depot alternative; oral haloperidol overlap for 4 weeks needed while depot levels establish gradually
options.rationale: Switching agents when the patient has been well controlled on paliperidone loses drug continuity; haloperidol decanoate carries higher EPS risk. Not the best approach when a matched depot exists. (Source: RANZCP; AMH)

options.text: Give a single loading dose of paliperidone palmitate 234 mg IM deltoid today only and cease oral paliperidone; a single loading dose achieves therapeutic levels without any need for the day-8 dose
options.rationale: Single-dose loading is not the approved paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly regimen; two-dose loading (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8) is required. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI)

options.text: Start paliperidone palmitate 3-monthly formulation now without prior use of the 1-monthly product; this is convenient given his adherence issues and avoids the need for monthly clinic visits
options.rationale: The 3-monthly formulation is only used after at least 4 months of stable dosing on 1-monthly paliperidone palmitate, not as an initial depot start. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI)

options.text: Give paliperidone palmitate 150 mg IM deltoid on day 1 and 100 mg IM deltoid on day 8; oral paliperidone can be ceased on day 1 without further oral overlap, with medication review at discharge
options.rationale: TGA-approved initiation for paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly uses a two-injection loading regimen (150 mg IM deltoid day 1, 100 mg IM deltoid day 8) which achieves therapeutic levels quickly enough that oral overlap is not required. This is a distinguishing feature versus most other depot antipsychotics which do require oral overlap. (Source: TGA paliperidone palmitate PI; TG Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Depot antipsychotic initiation varies by agent. Paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly uses a loading regimen (150 mg day 1, 100 mg day 8, both deltoid) that removes the need for oral overlap. Most other depots (risperidone LAI, flupentixol decanoate, zuclopenthixol decanoate) require oral overlap of 3-4 weeks. Aripiprazole LAI requires 14 days of oral aripiprazole overlap.
key_points: Paliperidone palmitate 1-monthly: 150 mg deltoid day 1, 100 mg deltoid day 8, no oral overlap needed
Risperidone LAI: 3-week oral overlap while depot levels establish
Aripiprazole LAI: 14 days oral aripiprazole overlap
3-monthly paliperidone palmitate only after 4 months stable on 1-monthly product
explanation.pearls: In context: check the specific depot's oral overlap requirement; paliperidone palmitate is a rare no-overlap exception because of its loading regimen.
